row.basis: break fallow ground; sow righteousness; harvest steadfast love
row.note: Commentary makes fieldwork a figure for growth into lasting good; Hosea directly joins breaking uncultivated soil and sowing justice to a harvest of love, adding a moral yield to the image.

row.basis: cleansing joined to multiplied grain
row.note: The commentary joins z-k-w's growth and purification senses; Ezekiel promises both rescue from uncleanness and multiplied grain, explicitly coupling moral cleansing with field abundance.

row.basis: God supplies seed and multiplies harvest of righteousness
row.note: Commentary links crop growth, giving, and purification; Paul says God supplies seed, increases it, and multiplies the harvest of righteousness, making generosity productive in righteousness.

row.basis: sowing generously and reaping generously
row.note: The commentary pictures a share given from growing produce; Paul makes generosity itself sowing whose return is measured at harvest, extending the crop image to giving.

row.basis: rain-fed land yields useful crop and receives blessing
row.note: Commentary contrasts cultivated yield with failed wild growth; Hebrews says land drinking rain and producing useful crops for cultivators is blessed, making productive reception of rain the positive outcome.

row.basis: thorns yield curse and burning
row.note: Against the commentary's cultivated crop that is harvested and its failing pasture, Hebrews' same rain-fed ground can instead bear thorns, be rejected, and end in burning; it sharpens the field's two outcomes.

row.basis: tithe brought to the storehouse; blessing poured out
row.note: The commentary describes a measured share given from produce; Malachi requires the full tithe and promises overflowing blessing, joining a crop's due to its continued abundance.

row.basis: devourer restrained; vine keeps its fruit
row.note: The commentary's due-paid crop leaves a clean remainder; after the tithe, Malachi says the destroyer will not ruin produce and the vine will not fail, explicitly protecting what remains.

row.basis: one plants, another waters, God gives growth
row.note: The commentary's field needs cultivation and growth; Paul distinguishes planting and watering from God's giving the increase, locating the crop's growth in divine care.

row.basis: God's field and fellow workers
row.note: The commentary reads Rabb through tending a farm; Paul calls the community God's field and its ministers God's coworkers, turning stewardship of a field into a communal image.

row.basis: first fruits from threshing floor, wine press, oxen, and sheep
row.note: The commentary describes a share of produce being given; the Didache specifies first fruits from harvest and livestock for prophets, or for the poor if no prophet is present, making the due a concrete communal practice.

row.basis: alms extinguish sin like water extinguishes fire
row.note: The commentary says the crop's given share purifies what remains; Sirach directly compares alms to water quenching fire and says it atones for sin, supplying a Jewish formulation of giving as purification.

row.basis: almsgiving purges sin
row.note: The commentary connects the paid share with cleansing; Tobit says almsgiving delivers from death and purges sin, explicitly giving charity a purifying and saving effect.

row.basis: the field corner has no fixed minimum measure
row.note: The commentary treats a known measured share as due from produce; Peah instead assigns a field's corner to the poor without a fixed minimum, showing a neighboring Jewish harvest due with a deliberately different measure.

row.basis: corners of the field and gleanings left for poor and sojourner
row.note: The commentary's grown crop yields a portion owed; Leviticus leaves field edges and gleanings for the poor and resident alien, making the share a right taken directly from harvest.

row.basis: vineyard gleanings and fallen grapes left for poor and sojourner
row.note: The commentary's due comes from a crop and purifies its remainder; Leviticus applies the same harvest rule to grapes, showing the share across a second cultivated product.

row.basis: a forgotten sheaf left for stranger, orphan, and widow
row.note: The commentary's field produces a share that is given; Deuteronomy assigns even an accidentally forgotten sheaf to vulnerable neighbors, specifying a harvest right rather than mere generosity.

row.basis: tithe of seed and fruit belongs to YHWH
row.note: The commentary's crop gives rise to a measured due; Leviticus marks the tithe of field seed and tree fruit as holy to YHWH, giving the agricultural share a sacred status.

row.basis: tithe of annual field increase
row.note: The commentary's crop yields a fixed share; Deuteronomy requires a tithe of all yearly seed-field produce, making the recurring harvest the basis of the due.

row.basis: third-year tithe stored in towns
row.note: The commentary describes measured yield paid out; Deuteronomy's third-year tithe is stored locally, setting aside produce for Levite and vulnerable neighbors.

row.basis: Levite, stranger, orphan, and widow eat and are satisfied
row.note: The commentary says the share given purifies what remains; this verse states who receives the stored tithe and that they eat their fill, adding the social result of the crop's due.

row.basis: first fruits presented before YHWH
row.note: The commentary's cultivated product has a right paid from it; Deuteronomy makes the first of the land's produce a presentation to YHWH, a distinct first-fruit form of the due.

row.basis: one fifth of the harvest given to Pharaoh; four fifths kept for seed and food
row.note: The commentary defines kharāj as a known annual amount removed from property; Joseph's statute assigns one fifth of Egypt's harvest to Pharaoh and leaves the rest to the cultivator, concretely pairing due and remainder.

row.basis: one fifth of produce established as a continuing land tax
row.note: The commentary links the crop's annual yield to a measured due; Genesis says Joseph made the one-fifth payment a standing statute, an unusually close fiscal counterpart to the commentary's fixed annual amount.

row.basis: Levites give a tenth of the tithe they receive
row.note: The commentary follows a share given from produce with what remains after payment; Numbers requires Levites to set aside a tenth of their own tithe, showing a due passed onward from a due.

row.basis: the Levites' offering counted as grain from threshing floor and wine from press
row.note: The commentary's share comes from harvested produce; Numbers explicitly treats the Levites' contribution as threshing-floor grain and wine-press yield, joining obligation to agricultural output.

row.basis: Isaac sows, reaps a hundredfold, and is blessed
row.note: The commentary joins seed growth to success; Isaac's literal sowing and hundredfold harvest in the same year are explicitly attributed to YHWH's blessing, giving the agricultural success a narrated instance.

row.basis: plowing and harrowing before sowing
row.note: The commentary says falāḥ names splitting the soil and the farmer who does it; Isaiah asks whether the plowman keeps plowing and opening the ground all day, directly placing soil-breaking before the crop.

row.basis: different seeds scattered after leveling the field
row.note: The commentary develops a worked field into growing produce; Isaiah describes leveling the surface and sowing distinct crops in their places, adding the ordered steps between plowing and yield.

row.basis: God waters furrows and softens ridges, blessing growth
row.note: The commentary links divine blessing to seed growth; the psalm depicts God saturating and leveling furrows and blessing their growth, making cultivation and increase part of God's care.

row.basis: the year crowned with goodness and abundance
row.note: The commentary joins success to remaining in good; the psalm says God crowns the year with goodness and abundance overflows, connecting agricultural yield with goodness across a whole year.

row.basis: pastures clothed and valleys covered with grain
row.note: The commentary contrasts failing pasture with cultivated produce; the psalm pictures pasture and valley alike clothed with flocks and grain, adding a scene of abundant land rather than withering grass.

row.basis: bread shared with the hungry and the homeless sheltered
row.note: The commentary says a share is given from one's product; Isaiah defines the fast through sharing bread and taking the poor into one's house, making the ethical claim on one's provision concrete.

row.basis: the generous person becomes a watered garden and unfailing spring
row.note: The commentary joins giving with growth and lasting good; Isaiah promises that the one guided by YHWH will be like a watered garden whose waters do not fail, making generosity's result enduring and fertile.

row.basis: rain makes earth bud, supplying seed to sower and bread to eater
row.note: The commentary says seed grows by God's blessing; Isaiah's rain and snow make the earth bud and provide both seed and bread, spelling out the movement from divine water to future sowing and present food.

row.basis: tree by water bears fruit, leaf does not wither, and prospers
row.note: The commentary links growth to success that remains in good; the psalm's planted tree bears fruit in season and does not wither, joining productive growth to persistence.

row.basis: human placed in garden to work and keep it
row.note: The commentary reads Rabb as undertaking the repair and care of a farm; Genesis gives the human the work of serving and guarding the garden, adding the cultivator's assigned stewardship.

row.basis: grass and flower fade, but God's word stands forever
row.note: The commentary contrasts pasture that perishes with the field yield that remains in good; Isaiah explicitly sets fading vegetation against what lasts forever, sharpening the contrast of transience and permanence.

row.basis: righteous flourish like palm and cedar planted in God's courts
row.note: The commentary joins success with growth that remains in good; the psalm makes the righteous flourish as long-lived planted trees, adding an image of rooted persistence.

row.basis: righteous still bear fruit in old age
row.note: The commentary links growth to enduring good; the psalm's righteous remain fresh and fruitful in old age, making continuing yield a sign of lasting vitality.

row.basis: God makes grass for cattle and plants for human food
row.note: The commentary contrasts pasture that fades with cultivated yield; the psalm says God makes grass for animals and plants humans cultivate for food, distinguishing provision for both pasture and field.

row.basis: uncultivated vine and spontaneous growth left unreaped in sabbath year
row.note: The commentary says wild pasture dries and is carried away while a worked field bears owed produce; Leviticus forbids harvesting spontaneous sabbath growth, assigning the unworked year's yield a protected use rather than treating it as waste.

row.basis: uncultivated yield is food for domestic and wild animals
row.note: The commentary contrasts fading pasture with fruitful cultivation; Leviticus makes the sabbath land's spontaneous growth food for animals, a different valuation of land left unworked.

row.basis: vineyard owner digs, clears stones, plants vines, and expects grapes
row.note: The commentary describes a field being worked for its product; Isaiah's owner prepares a vineyard carefully but gets wild grapes, making failed yield a narrative counterpoint to the crop whose due is paid.

row.basis: vineyard stands for Israel; God sought justice and found bloodshed
row.note: The commentary's field image connects produce with what is rightly owed; Isaiah interprets the vineyard's failed fruit as Israel's failure of justice, adding an ethical measure to agricultural yield.

row.basis: Israel's mountains will bear branches and fruit for the people
row.note: The commentary's planted field grows and yields its product; Ezekiel promises the restored land will branch and bear fruit for Israel, making field fertility a sign of restoration.

row.basis: God restores the years eaten by locusts
row.note: The commentary contrasts a pasture that dries and disappears with enduring yield; Joel promises the crop years consumed by locusts will be restored, offering a recovery from agricultural loss.

row.basis: one scatters freely and yet increases
row.note: The commentary joins giving a portion to continued increase; Proverbs says one who scatters freely grows richer, directly pairing generosity with growth while leaving the mechanism proverbial.

row.basis: the generous person is enriched and the waterer watered
row.note: The commentary joins crop growth to a share given; Proverbs says the one who refreshes others will be refreshed, extending the field's reciprocity into an ethical maxim.

row.basis: good soil hears and bears a crop at differing yields
row.note: The commentary pictures a worked field whose crop grows and is harvested; Jesus interprets good soil as hearing and bearing fruit, with thirty-, sixty-, or hundredfold yield, making receptivity and productivity explicit.

row.basis: good soil holds the word and bears fruit with patience
row.note: The commentary joins growth to lasting good; Luke's good soil holds the word in an honest heart and bears fruit with endurance, linking soil, inner purification, and persistence.

row.basis: seed grows while the farmer sleeps and rises
row.note: The commentary says the crop grows through divine blessing; Mark's farmer does not know how the seed sprouts and grows, emphasizing growth not controlled by the cultivator.

row.basis: grain ripe, the sickle is put in because harvest has come
row.note: The commentary's success becomes a lasting crop; Mark's parable ends with ripe grain and harvest, supplying the endpoint of the growth process.

row.basis: fruit-bearing branch is pruned so it bears more fruit
row.note: The commentary joins purification with crop increase; Jesus uses καθαίρει, a verb for pruning or cleansing, of the already fruitful branch, explicitly meeting purification and increased fruit.

row.basis: vineyard owner prepares the vineyard and leases it to tenants
row.note: The commentary reads Rabb as one who undertakes a property's repair and care; Jesus' owner plants, fences, equips, and leases a vineyard, a close scene of the cultivator's stewardship.

row.basis: owner sends servants to collect the vineyard's produce
row.note: The commentary says the crop has a due portion; the vineyard owner sends servants at harvest to receive its fruit, making the owner's claim on cultivated yield explicit.

row.basis: sowing to the Spirit reaps eternal life
row.note: The commentary joins a cultivated yield with what is better and more enduring; Paul makes sowing to the Spirit yield eternal life, transferring the harvest to the afterlife.

row.basis: rains and fruitful seasons fill people with food and gladness
row.note: The commentary attributes growth to divine blessing; Paul points to God giving rain and fruitful seasons, joining crop provision with nourishment and joy.

row.basis: generosity lays up a foundation for the future and real life
row.note: The commentary links paying the crop's due with what lasts; Timothy's instruction joins generosity to a future foundation and taking hold of life, giving the share an explicitly lasting horizon.

row.basis: the seed sown in earth and its emergence as an image of resurrection
row.note: The commentary contrasts perishing pasture with the crop that remains; Clement points to seed put in earth and its subsequent growth as evidence for resurrection, connecting agricultural persistence with life beyond death.

row.basis: no rain and no human to work the ground
row.note: The commentary's field requires both growth and tending; Genesis says vegetation had not appeared because YHWH had not sent rain and there was no human to work the ground, giving a compact account of those conditions.

row.basis: desert becomes fruitful field when the spirit is poured out
row.note: The commentary contrasts withered pasture with worked, productive land; Isaiah says wilderness becomes a fruitful field after the spirit is poured out, making transformed fertility a restoration image.

row.basis: celebration with Levite and sojourner over the land's good produce
row.note: The commentary's harvest share is given to another; Deuteronomy commands rejoicing with Levite and stranger in the good YHWH gave, showing the produce's due ending in shared enjoyment.

row.basis: rain brings grain, wine, and oil
row.note: The commentary attributes crop growth to blessing and God's care; Deuteronomy promises rain in its season and the resulting harvest, making rainfall the condition of the land's produce.

row.basis: olive tree beaten once; remainder left for stranger, orphan, and widow
row.note: The commentary's share comes from a product while a remainder is kept; Deuteronomy limits harvesting olives to one pass so a remnant remains for vulnerable people, making restraint part of the due.

row.basis: vineyard gleaning left for stranger, orphan, and widow
row.note: The commentary's crop yields a share for another; this verse applies the remnant rule to grapes, showing the harvest right in a third crop.

row.basis: Arabic source label ز ك و and Hebrew זכה; speaker says he purified his heart in vain
row.note: The commentary labels Arabic z-k-w for purification as well as growth; the psalmist uses Hebrew זכה for keeping his heart pure and pairs it with washing his hands, a cognate used for purity amid a crisis of reward.

row.basis: Arabic source label ز ك و and Hebrew זכה; who can claim a clean heart?
row.note: The commentary connects purification to paying a crop's due; Proverbs uses Hebrew זכה to ask who can claim to have made the heart pure from sin, focusing the cognate on moral cleanness.

row.basis: Arabic source label ز ك و and Hebrew זכה; can a mortal be pure before God?
row.note: The commentary uses z-k-w for purification; Job uses Hebrew זכה in asking whether a human can be pure, adding a skeptical limit on claims of self-cleansing.

row.basis: Arabic source label ز ك و and Hebrew זכה; how can a human be justified and clean before God?
row.note: The commentary links purification with the crop's paid share; Bildad uses Hebrew זכה in questioning human purity before God, a cognate that frames cleansing as a divine rather than merely accounting matter.

row.basis: break up fallow ground and do not sow among thorns
row.note: The commentary's farmer splits and works the earth; Jeremiah uses plowing fallow ground as a call to change before sowing, making the fieldwork an ethical demand.

row.basis: sowing in tears and reaping in joy
row.note: The commentary makes a crop's growth culminate in good that lasts; the psalm's mournful sowing gives way to joyful harvest, adding reversal from present labor to future reward.

row.basis: plowman overtakes reaper in a season of abundance
row.note: The commentary's growth is a field's enduring success; Amos depicts grain harvest and grape harvest overlapping, intensifying the crop image into restored abundance.

row.basis: heavens shut, rain withheld, and land's produce lost
row.note: The commentary contrasts a field that grows and yields its due with a pasture that fades; Deuteronomy describes the inverse, disobedience bringing no rain and a land that fails to produce.

row.basis: almsgiving and cleanness; rendering of the Greek is disputed
row.note: The commentary says a paid share purifies what remains; Luke's difficult instruction is commonly read as giving alms from what is within and says all is clean, directly associating alms with cleanness while the exact wording is uncertain.

row.basis: weeds gathered for burning while wheat is stored at harvest
row.note: The commentary distinguishes failing wild growth from a cultivated crop that is gathered; Jesus' parable separates weeds for burning from wheat for the barn, making the different harvest fates explicit.

row.basis: murderous tenants refuse the owner's share and lose the vineyard
row.note: The commentary's successful field grows, pays its due, and leaves a remainder; the tenants withhold the owner's fruit and are displaced, turning unpaid produce into a judgment story.

row.basis: fruit-producing people receive the kingdom
row.note: The commentary links fruitful purification with the lasting hereafter; Jesus says the kingdom goes to a people producing its fruits, giving the vineyard's yield an ethical and eschatological measure.

row.basis: rich farmer stores his abundant harvest for many years
row.note: The commentary's field yields product but asks what is lasting; the rich farmer plans to keep his grain for years, setting accumulated crop beside the commentary's question of enduring good.

row.basis: the farmer dies that night and loses his stored goods
row.note: The commentary calls the hereafter better and more lasting than worldly life; the farmer's sudden death interrupts his plan to keep the harvest, making stored produce an unstable remainder.

row.basis: rich toward oneself versus rich toward God
row.note: The commentary ties success to enduring good; Jesus concludes that accumulating goods without being rich toward God misses the lasting measure of success.

row.basis: fruit leading to sanctification and its end, eternal life
row.note: The commentary brings purification and lasting success together; Paul says liberation bears fruit in sanctification and ends in eternal life, giving the ethical fruit an enduring destination.

row.basis: farmer waits patiently for precious earth's fruit and early and late rain
row.note: The commentary presents lasting good as the result of crop growth; James makes a farmer's patience for the precious harvest an example of waiting, adding the time required for yield.

row.basis: bread cast on waters found after many days
row.note: The commentary links a present share with what remains; Ecclesiastes uses casting bread on waters and finding it later, a possible giving-and-return image whose precise sense is debated.

row.basis: grain that dies bears much fruit
row.note: The commentary sets a fading pasture against growth that yields; Jesus' grain image makes loss precede abundant fruit, a specific but differently focused reversal.

row.basis: body sown perishable and raised imperishable
row.note: The commentary opposes perishing pasture to what remains; Paul uses sowing and resurrection to contrast perishable and imperishable bodies, extending the crop's persistence to resurrection.

row.basis: seedtime and harvest continue as long as the earth remains
row.note: The commentary makes crop growth culminate in what remains; Genesis promises that seedtime and harvest will not cease while the earth remains, giving the agricultural cycle an explicit duration.

row.basis: Ruth asks to glean ears of grain in a field
row.note: The commentary treats a share from the crop as a right given; Ruth's request and gleaning in Boaz's field narrate a vulnerable foreign widow receiving harvest produce under Israel's field practice.

row.basis: workers pull grain from bundles and leave it for Ruth to glean
row.note: The commentary's field yields an owed portion; Boaz orders extra grain deliberately left for Ruth, showing a landowner expanding the harvest share through generous care.

row.basis: the king takes a tenth of seed and vineyard produce
row.note: The commentary defines kharāj as a known amount removed from property each year; Samuel warns that a king will take a tenth of grain and vineyard yield, a political levy that makes the fixed crop share a contested claim.

row.basis: openhanded aid to the poor is followed by blessing on all work
row.note: The commentary connects giving a crop share with cleansing and remaining good; Deuteronomy commands giving to the poor and promises blessing on the giver's work, joining generosity to productive success.

row.basis: honor YHWH with wealth and first fruits of all produce
row.note: The commentary's harvest has a portion due; Proverbs makes first fruits the way to honor YHWH, identifying agricultural priority as a form of payment and devotion.

row.basis: full barns and overflowing wine vats follow first fruits
row.note: The commentary says the given share purifies the remainder; Proverbs places full barns and vats after first-fruit honor, giving a direct promise of abundance alongside the due.

row.basis: seed of peace, fruitful vine, productive ground, and dew
row.note: The commentary joins field growth to good that lasts; Zechariah brings seed, vine, land produce, and dew together as a restored blessing, combining crop fertility with peace.

row.basis: tree by water stays green in heat and never ceases bearing fruit
row.note: The commentary contrasts pasture that dries with productive growth that remains; Jeremiah's water-rooted tree does not fear drought and keeps yielding fruit, making endurance explicit.

row.basis: earth yields increase and God blesses
row.note: The commentary attributes growth to divine blessing; the psalm says the earth has yielded its increase and God blesses, directly joining harvest and blessing.

row.basis: distributes freely to the poor; righteousness endures forever
row.note: The commentary links the crop's given share to lasting good; the psalm joins generous distribution to the poor with righteousness that endures, a close ethical counterpart to a purifying share and permanent success.

row.basis: first-ripe barley loaves are brought to Elisha
row.note: The commentary's yield has a portion paid out; a man brings first-fruit barley bread to the prophet, narrating produce set aside as a sacred share.

row.basis: a small barley offering feeds a hundred with some left over
row.note: The commentary follows a crop's given share with what remains; Elisha distributes the offering, a hundred eat, and food remains, adding miraculous increase and remainder to the harvest image.

row.basis: one-sixth ephah from each homer of wheat and barley
row.note: The commentary defines the annual kharāj as a known amount removed from property; Ezekiel specifies a measured grain contribution, an exact agricultural counterpart to a fixed due.

row.basis: oil contribution measured against the homer
row.note: The commentary's crop share is measured and paid; Ezekiel likewise sets an oil contribution by a defined volume, extending measured dues from grain to another product.

row.basis: do not plow injustice or sow its furrows, lest you reap it manyfold
row.note: The commentary makes plowing and growth a figure for success; Sirach turns furrowing and reaping into moral consequence, adding a warning that unjust cultivation multiplies its own return.

row.basis: charity as the salt that preserves wealth
row.note: The commentary says a paid share purifies what remains; the rabbinic saying calls charity the salt of wealth, interpreting giving as what preserves a person's remaining property.

row.basis: bear fruit worthy of repentance
row.note: The commentary joins purification to a productive crop; John demands fruit that fits repentance, making agricultural yield an observable ethical consequence of cleansing.

row.basis: share a second tunic and food with someone who has none
row.note: The commentary says a portion from one's produce is given; John's answer turns repentance into sharing clothing and food, making the purifying act materially concrete.

row.basis: tax collectors must collect no more than the assigned amount
row.note: The commentary defines kharāj as a known amount taken from property; John tells tax collectors not to collect beyond what is ordered, making fixed dues an ethical boundary against extraction.

row.basis: tithing herbs while neglecting justice, mercy, and faith
row.note: The commentary links paying a crop's share to purification; Jesus says exact tithing must not displace justice, mercy, and faith, qualifying the claim that payment alone cleans the remainder.

row.basis: first blade, then ear, then full grain on the stalk
row.note: The commentary unfolds soil-breaking into seed growth and lasting yield; Mark specifies the intermediate stages of that growth before the ripe harvest, preserving the crop's full sequence.

row.basis: the plowman plows in hope and the thresher hopes to share the crop
row.note: The commentary names the farmer through breaking soil and gives the crop a due share; Paul says agricultural workers labor in hope of sharing the produce, directly joining cultivation and right to yield.

row.basis: gift to Paul becomes fruit increasing to the giver's account
row.note: The commentary links the crop's paid share to lasting good; Paul calls the Philippians' material gift fruit accruing to their account, recasting generosity as a yield that lasts.

row.basis: all flesh is grass and its glory like a flower that fades
row.note: The commentary contrasts perishing pasture with lasting good; Peter applies Isaiah's grass-and-flower image to human life, making the pasture's decay a figure for mortal transience.

row.basis: the Lord's word remains forever and is the preached gospel
row.note: The commentary sets fading growth against what endures; Peter continues the grass quotation by identifying the enduring word with the gospel preached to the audience, giving Isaiah's plant contrast a Christian proclamation context.

row.basis: earth sprouts and garden makes seed grow; righteousness and praise spring up
row.note: The commentary joins crop growth to purification and success; Isaiah compares the earth's sprouting to righteousness and praise springing before nations, bringing agricultural and ethical growth together.

row.basis: field grass is alive today and thrown into the oven tomorrow, yet clothed by God
row.note: The commentary uses withering pasture as the transient outcome; Jesus also makes field grass short-lived, but uses God's care for it to argue trust, giving ephemeral growth a positive theological value.

row.basis: God gives each seed its own body
row.note: The commentary attributes seed growth to divine blessing; Paul says God gives the seed its body as God wills, making the source of differentiated growth explicitly divine.

row.basis: tree of life bears monthly fruit and its leaves heal nations
row.note: The commentary links growth with what remains good; Revelation's final-city tree yields continually and heals the nations, giving enduring fruit an afterlife setting.
